claim: Two adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) performed a direction discrimination task with post-decision wagering (PDW).
source: Two adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) performed a direction discrimination task with post-decision wagering (PDW, Figure 1A), as described previously (Fetsch et al., 2014a; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Zylberberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects and task design.

claim: Monkeys chose the sure-bet most frequently when the motion was weak.
source: As in previous studies (Fetsch et al., 2014a; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Zylberberg et al., 2016), monkeys chose the sure-bet most frequently when the motion was weak (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Monkeys chose the sure-bet most frequently when motion was of short duration.
source: As in previous studies (Fetsch et al., 2014a; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Zylberberg et al., 2016), monkeys chose the sure-bet most frequently when the motion was weak (Figure 1B) and of short duration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Monkeys' accuracy was greater when the sure-bet was available but waived, versus when it was unavailable (p<10−10).
source: their accuracy was greater when the sure-bet was available but waived, versus when it was unavailable (Figure 1C; p<10−10, logistic regression)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (logistic regression) of behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At least 8 weeks before commencing experiments, area MT in one hemisphere of each animal was injected with an AAV vector to drive expression of Jaws under the control of the CaMKIIα promoter.
source: At least 8 weeks before commencing experiments, area MT in one hemisphere of each animal was injected with an AAV vector to drive expression of the red light-sensitive chloride pump Jaws (cruxhalorhodopsin; Chuong et al., 2014) under the control of the CaMKIIα promoter.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure for viral vector injection.

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis in a third animal revealed robust Jaws-GFP expression in superficial and deep layers following injections in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP).
source: This analysis revealed robust Jaws-GFP expression in superficial and deep layers (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The AAV-CaMKIIα-Jaws vector showed tropism for excitatory pyramidal cells.
source: This analysis revealed robust Jaws-GFP expression in superficial and deep layers (Figure 2A), and a tropism for excitatory pyramidal cells (Figure 2B), as shown in previous studies using the CaMKIIα promoter (Han et al., 2009; Nassi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B and comparison to previous studies.

claim: 9% of Jaws-GFP-positive neurons (83 of 903) were double-labeled for the inhibitory marker parvalbumin, giving an upper bound on selectivity of 91%.
source: This tropism was not as strong as in previous work: 9% of Jaws-GFP-positive neurons (83 of 903) were double-labeled for the inhibitory marker parvalbumin (Figure 2B), giving an upper bound on selectivity of 91%
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Single-unit visual responses to high-coherence RDM stimuli presented at the preferred direction and speed were strongly suppressed on average (N = 26).
source: Single-unit visual responses to high-coherence RDM stimuli—presented at the preferred direction and speed—were strongly suppressed on average (N = 26; Figure 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by single-unit recording data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Among putative Jaws-expressing neurons, the visually evoked response, after subtracting baseline activity, was suppressed by 101% (±13% SEM; N = 20).
source: Among putative Jaws-expressing neurons, the visually evoked response, after subtracting baseline activity, was suppressed by 101% (±13% SEM; N = 20; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of single-unit recording data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Without baseline subtraction, the average firing rate during stimulus presentation was reduced by 72% ± 5%.
source: Without baseline subtraction, the average firing rate during stimulus presentation was reduced by 72% ± 5%.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the degree of neural suppression.

claim: MU responses during the discrimination task were reduced by an average of 33% (±0.3% SEM, N = 20058 trials).
source: In contrast, MU responses during the discrimination task were reduced by an average of 33% (±0.3% SEM, N = 20058 trials; Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by multi-unit recording data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Photosuppression caused a modest but significant choice bias in the predicted direction when the degree of suppression was greater than about 45% (shift = −2.1% coh±0.6% SE; p=0.001).
source: This analysis (Figure 4B) showed that photosuppression caused a modest but significant choice bias in the predicted direction, provided that the degree of suppression was greater than about 45% (Figure 4C; shift = −2.1% coh±0.6% SE; p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: The largest effects on confidence were observed when suppression was strong (shift = −2.9% ± 1.4%, p=0.03).
source: The relationship between ∆R and the effect on confidence was more complex (Figure 4B, blue trace), but the largest effects were also observed when suppression was strong (Figure 4D; shift = −2.9% ± 1.4%, p=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figures 4B and 4D.

claim: Systematic biases on laser trials appeared early within a session and dissipated over the course of tens of minutes (100–500 trials).
source: However, while collecting the data we noticed a tendency for systematic biases on laser trials to appear early within a session, only to dissipate over the course of tens of minutes (100–500 trials; ~5 s per trial on average, including intertrial intervals).
evidence: This is a direct observation about temporal dynamics of behavioral effects.

claim: Over the first 500 trials of an example session, the monkey tended to choose the preferred direction less often on laser trials vs. no-laser trials, effectively shifting the psychometric curve to the right (shift = −4.6%, p=0.14).
source: Over the first 500 trials, the monkey tended to choose the preferred direction less often on laser trials vs. no-laser trials, effectively shifting the psychometric curve to the right (Figure 5A; shift = −4.6%, p=0.14, Equation 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of behavioral data from an example session shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the remaining ~1000 trials of the example session, there was essentially no effect on choices (shift = −0.7% coh, p=0.75).
source: In contrast, there was essentially no effect on choices in the remaining ~1000 trials of the session (Figure 5B; shift = −0.7% coh, p=0.75).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of behavioral data from an example session shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Pooling across all sessions with enough trials to measure it (minimum 800 trials per session, N = 10 sessions) showed rightward shifts early in the session (choice shift = −3.5% coh±1.1%, p=0.001; confidence shift = −3.8% ± 1.9%, p=0.05).
source: This trend was evident when pooling across all sessions with enough trials to measure it (minimum 800 trials per session, N = 10 sessions): rightward shifts early in the session (choice shift = −3.5% coh±1.1%, p=0.001, Figure 5A'; confidence shift = −3.8% ± 1.9% [Equation 3], p=0.05, Figure 5C')
evidence: This claim is supported by pooled analysis of behavioral data shown in Figures 5A' and 5C'.

claim: Later in sessions, there were no significant shifts (choice shift = −0.7%, p=0.26; confidence shift = 0.1%, p=0.93).
source: but not later (choice shift = −0.7%, p=0.26, Figure 5B'; confidence shift = 0.1%, p=0.93; Figure 5D').
evidence: This claim is supported by pooled analysis of behavioral data shown in Figures 5B' and 5D'.

claim: The difference between early and late trials was statistically significant for choice (p=0.01) and confidence (p=0.02, Bonferroni corrected).
source: Post-hoc tests using generalized linear models (Equation 5, see Materials and methods) showed that the difference between early and late trials was statistically significant for choice (p=0.01) and confidence (p=0.02, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using generalized linear models.

claim: The decrease in effectiveness of photosuppression on behavior was not accompanied by an attenuation of its effect on neural responses.
source: In our case, however, the decrease in effectiveness of photosuppression on behavior was not accompanied by an attenuation of its effect on neural responses.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing behavioral and neural effects over time.

claim: In the example session, the degree of suppression was slightly greater in early versus late trials (∆R = −0.80 ± 0.01 and −0.74 ± 0.01, respectively; p<0.05).
source: In the example session (Figure 5E vs. Figure 5F), the degree of suppression was slightly greater in early versus late trials (∆R = −0.80 ± 0.01 and −0.74 ± 0.01, respectively; p<0.05, bootstrap confidence interval, resampling trials with replacement)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of neural data from an example session shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Across all 10 sessions in the pooled dataset, the trend was toward greater suppression on late trials (∆R early = −0.28 ± 0.008, late = −0.40 ± 0.004, p<0.05).
source: Across all 10 sessions in the pooled dataset (Figure 5E' vs. Figure 5F') the trend was in the opposite direction, toward greater suppression on late trials (∆R early = −0.28 ± 0.008, late = −0.40 ± 0.004, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by pooled analysis of neural data shown in Figures 5E' and 5F'.

claim: The behavioral effects of photosuppression were largely restricted to trials with short and intermediate durations (duration <~350 ms).
source: Remarkably, we found that the behavioral effects of photosuppression were largely restricted to trials with short and intermediate durations (duration <~350 ms; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of behavioral data as a function of stimulus duration shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Short-duration trials exhibited light-induced shifts of −4.7% (p=0.0006) for choice and −5.7% (p=0.004) for confidence.
source: Short-duration trials exhibited light-induced shifts of −4.7% (p=0.0006, Figure 7A) and −5.7% (p=0.004, Figure 7C) for choice and confidence respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figures 7A and 7C.

claim: Long-duration trials showed no systematic biases in either choice (−0.6%, p=0.50) or confidence (0.38%, p=0.84).
source: whereas long-duration trials showed no systematic biases in either measure (choice: −0.6%, p=0.50; confidence: 0.38%, p=0.84).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the absence of behavioral effects on long-duration trials.

claim: The effect of duration was statistically significant for confidence (p=0.002, Bonferroni corrected) and marginally so for choice (p=0.04).
source: The effect of duration was statistically significant (Equation 5, Materials and methods) for confidence (p=0.002, Bonferroni corrected) and marginally so for choice (p=0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using generalized linear models.

claim: The sub-second attenuation of behavioral effects was not readily explained by differences in MT neural responses on short- versus long-duration trials.
source: As with the slower form of compensation, this sub-second attenuation of behavioral effects was not readily explained by differences in MT neural responses on short- versus long-duration trials (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing behavioral and neural effects as a function of trial duration.

claim: Neuronal sensitivity was greater on long-duration trials when including all spiking activity throughout the stimulus epoch (neuronal threshold = 27.2 ± 1.6% coh versus 37.5 ± 2.5% for short durations).
source: Unsurprisingly, neuronal sensitivity was greater on long-duration trials when including all spiking activity throughout the stimulus epoch (neuronal threshold = 27.2 ± 1.6% coh versus 37.5 ± 2.5% for short durations; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about neuronal sensitivity based on ROC analysis.

claim: Activity early in the stimulus epoch was suppressed equally on short- and long-duration trials.
source: Indeed, any candidate explanation for this result must contend with the fact that activity early in the stimulus epoch was suppressed equally on short- and long-duration trials (Figure 7E vs. 7F), yet only the former showed behavioral effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of neural data shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: Unlike photosuppression, the biases in choice and confidence induced by µStim remained stable throughout the behavioral session.
source: Unlike photosuppression, and contrary to the findings of Salzman et al. (1992), the biases in choice and confidence induced by µStim remained stable throughout the behavioral session (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of microstimulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and comparison to previous work.

claim: The results demonstrate that systematic behavioral effects of optogenetic manipulation in nonhuman primates are achievable even when targeting neural populations on a small spatial scale.
source: The results demonstrate that systematic behavioral effects of optogenetic manipulation in nonhuman primates are achievable even when this requires the targeting of neural populations on a small spatial scale, that of cortical columns or clusters of neurons with similar functional properties.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the main finding of the study.

claim: Photosuppression in MT biased the animal's choices away from the preferred direction.
source: Photosuppression in MT biased the animal's choices away from the preferred direction, and also altered confidence in a way that mimics a change in motion strength (i.e., a rightward shift of the bell-shaped curve describing sure-bet choices as a function of coherence).
evidence: This is a summary statement about the behavioral effects of photosuppression.

claim: Photosuppression altered confidence in a way that mimics a change in motion strength.
source: Photosuppression in MT biased the animal's choices away from the preferred direction, and also altered confidence in a way that mimics a change in motion strength (i.e., a rightward shift of the bell-shaped curve describing sure-bet choices as a function of coherence).
evidence: This is a summary statement about the effects of photosuppression on confidence.

claim: The effects of photosuppression on choice and confidence were reasonably well matched as a function of the degree of suppression.
source: The effects were reasonably well matched as a function of the degree of suppression (Figure 4B), and they dissipated over a similar time course, both across (Figure 6A) and within trials (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of behavioral effects shown in Figures 4B, 6A, and 6B.

claim: The effects of photosuppression on choice and confidence dissipated over a similar time course, both across and within trials.
source: The effects were reasonably well matched as a function of the degree of suppression (Figure 4B), and they dissipated over a similar time course, both across (Figure 6A) and within trials (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal analysis of behavioral effects shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: The results are consistent with a role for MT neurons in providing a shared source of evidence supporting both choice and confidence.
source: These results are consistent with a role for MT neurons in providing a shared source of evidence supporting both aspects of a decision.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the pattern of behavioral effects.

claim: The results suggest a form of compensation or down-weighting of MT signals by downstream areas that are reading out this activity to form a decision.
source: Instead, the results suggest a compensatory change in the downstream readout of MT neural signals to reduce or nullify the effects of photosuppression on a time scale of 10–40 minutes.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the dissipation of behavioral effects without corresponding changes in neural suppression.

claim: The decision in the task is rendered with a saccadic eye movement, so the readout (and hence compensation) likely involves a network of areas including the lateral intraparietal area, frontal eye field, and superior colliculus.
source: Because the decision in our task is rendered with a saccadic eye movement, the readout (and hence compensation) likely involves a network of areas including the lateral intraparietal area, frontal eye field, and superior colliculus, although probably by way of the thalamus rather than direct projections from MT.
evidence: This is an inference based on known anatomy and the nature of the behavioral task.

claim: In the experiments, the reward rate was about 4% greater on laser trials compared to no-laser trials.
source: However, in our experiments the reward rate was about 4% greater on laser trials compared to no-laser trials, owing to the small magnitude of the bias and the subtle increase in sensitivity.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about reward rates in the experiment.

claim: The capacity of cortical circuits to compensate for artificially induced activity patterns may be greater for photosuppression compared to µStim.
source: This result implies that the capacity of cortical circuits to compensate for artificially induced activity patterns may be greater for photosuppression compared to µStim, although we cannot ascertain whether the key difference is the sign (suppression versus stimulation) or the modality (optogenetic versus electrical) of the perturbation.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on comparison of photosuppression and microstimulation effects.

claim: The suppressed activity is sensed as anomalous or unreliable by downstream circuitry.
source: Instead, the results motivate the hypothesis that the suppressed activity is sensed as anomalous or unreliable by downstream circuitry.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the fast compensation observed in the data.

claim: Unlike µStim, the suppression of cortical tissue might have an effect that is analogous to diaschisis, triggering a reconfiguration of functional connectivity in downstream networks.
source: That is, unlike µStim, the suppression of cortical tissue might have an effect that is analogous to diaschisis (Carrera and Tononi, 2014; Otchy et al., 2015), triggering a reconfiguration of functional connectivity in downstream networks.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on comparison to diaschisis and cited literature.

claim: This reconfiguration could cause structures involved in decision making to consult other sources of evidence, either elsewhere in MT or from other visual areas (e.g., MST, V3a, or V4).
source: This reconfiguration could cause structures involved in decision making to consult other sources of evidence, either elsewhere in MT or from other visual areas (e.g., MST, V3a, or V4).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of compensation.

claim: The nullification of behavioral effects of photosuppression on two distinct time scales invites caution when interpreting inactivation experiments that fail to affect behavior.
source: The nullification of behavioral effects of photosuppression on two distinct time scales (Figures 5–7) invites caution when interpreting inactivation experiments that fail to affect behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the implications of the findings for experimental design.

claim: For other areas and tasks that have not been extensively studied, it may be difficult to rule out compensation by circuits that perform the same or similar function.
source: A key role for MT in visual motion discrimination is not in doubt (but see Liu and Pack, 2017), but for other areas and tasks that have not been extensively studied, or where the results are more equivocal, it may be difficult to rule out compensation by circuits that perform the same or similar function (e.g., de Lafuente et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the broader implications of the findings, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Compensation can operate on a faster time scale than previously appreciated.
source: The present study suggests that this compensation can operate on a faster time scale than previously appreciated, further advocating the use of rigorous behavioral methods to identify the appropriate time scale for a perturbation.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the temporal dynamics of compensation observed in the study.

claim: Neurons in motion-sensitive cortical areas, especially the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas, are well suited to provide the evidence for the motion discrimination task.
source: Neurons in motion-sensitive cortical areas, especially the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas, are well suited to provide the evidence for the task, and theoretical considerations (Gold and Shadlen, 2001; Shadlen et al., 1996) point toward a simple and plausible computation: the subtraction of spike counts (or rates) between pools of neurons favoring each of the direction alternatives.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional properties of MT/MST neurons in relation to the task, supported by citations.

claim: Theoretical considerations point toward a simple and plausible computation: the subtraction of spike counts (or rates) between pools of neurons favoring each of the direction alternatives.
source: Neurons in motion-sensitive cortical areas, especially the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas, are well suited to provide the evidence for the task, and theoretical considerations (Gold and Shadlen, 2001; Shadlen et al., 1996) point toward a simple and plausible computation: the subtraction of spike counts (or rates) between pools of neurons favoring each of the direction alternatives.
evidence: This is a statement about theoretical models of decision making, supported by citations.

claim: This difference furnishes a quantity proportional to the log likelihood ratio favoring a given alternative, a statistical measure of the weight of evidence that can be accumulated over time to support optimal statistical decision making.
source: This difference furnishes a quantity proportional to the log likelihood ratio favoring a given alternative, a statistical measure of the weight of evidence that can be accumulated over time to support optimal statistical decision making (Gold and Shadlen, 2002; Wald, 1947)
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical interpretation of neural activity differences, supported by citations.

claim: Ditterich et al. (2003) demonstrated the specific differencing-and-integration mechanism that was previously hypothesized on theoretical grounds using electrical microstimulation.
source: Building on the work of Newsome and colleagues (Celebrini and Newsome, 1995; Salzman et al., 1992), Ditterich et al. (2003) took advantage of the columnar organization of MT (Albright et al., 1984) to demonstrate, beyond simply a causal role for these neurons in the task, the specific differencing-and-integration mechanism that was previously hypothesized on theoretical grounds.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Using electrical microstimulation to activate neurons largely within a single direction column, Ditterich et al. confirmed earlier reports showing that monkeys' choices were biased toward the preferred direction of the activated neurons.
source: Using electrical microstimulation (µStim) to activate neurons that were largely within a single direction column, they confirmed earlier reports showing that monkeys' choices were biased toward the preferred direction of the activated neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings.

claim: µStim increased the speed of decisions in favor of the preferred direction while slowing decisions made in favor of the opposite direction.
source: More importantly, µStim increased the speed of decisions in favor of the preferred direction while slowing decisions made in favor of the opposite direction.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings.

claim: The results of Ditterich et al. supported a model in which the decision is formed by temporal integration of momentary evidence, defined as the difference in activity of pools of MT neurons tuned for the preferred and anti-preferred motion direction.
source: The results supported a model in which the decision is formed by temporal integration of momentary evidence, defined as the difference in activity of pools of MT neurons tuned for the preferred and anti-preferred motion direction (Ditterich et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Decision confidence is affected by µStim in a way that is quantitatively commensurate with the effect on choices and well explained by a bounded evidence accumulation model.
source: More recently, we showed that decision confidence is affected by µStim in a way that is quantitatively commensurate with the effect on choices and well explained by a bounded evidence accumulation model (Fetsch et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: A common process of evidence accumulation underlies all three behavioral measures of decision making in this task: choice, reaction time, and confidence.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that a common process of evidence accumulation underlies all three behavioral measures of decision making in this task: choice, reaction time, and confidence.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on previous research findings.

claim: Reversible inactivation offers an important complement to stimulation for understanding the necessity of neural activity for driving behavior.
source: Causal activation of neurons informs our understanding of the sufficiency, but not the necessity, of neural activity for driving behavior. Thus, reversible inactivation offers an important complement to stimulation, but conventional methods in primate neuroscience (e.g., muscimol or cooling) are lacking in both spatial and temporal resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for using inactivation methods.

claim: Conventional methods of reversible inactivation in primate neuroscience (e.g., muscimol or cooling) are lacking in both spatial and temporal resolution.
source: Thus, reversible inactivation offers an important complement to stimulation, but conventional methods in primate neuroscience (e.g., muscimol or cooling) are lacking in both spatial and temporal resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of conventional inactivation methods.

claim: The temporal component of perturbations is crucial and often neglected.
source: The temporal component is crucial and often neglected.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of temporal specificity in causal manipulations.

claim: The insights gained from the µStim studies depended on targeting the perturbation not only to the appropriate neurons but also the appropriate time frame within a trial.
source: Indeed, the insights gained from the µStim studies described above depended on targeting the perturbation not only to the appropriate neurons but also the appropriate time frame within a trial (Seidemann et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of temporal specificity in previous research, supported by citation.

claim: µStim has drawbacks including the possibility of antidromic activation, the generation of unwanted temporal and spatial patterns of inactivation, and the difficulty of quantifying concurrent changes in neural activity due to voltage artifacts.
source: µStim itself has other drawbacks, including the possibility of antidromic activation, the generation of unwanted temporal and spatial patterns of inactivation (Butovas and Schwarz, 2003; Logothetis et al., 2010; Seidemann et al., 2002), and the difficulty of quantifying concurrent changes in neural activity due to voltage artifacts (but see Gnadt et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of microstimulation, supported by citations.

claim: An optogenetic approach was used to suppress MT activity during a motion discrimination task with post-decision wagering.
source: To address these limitations, we used an optogenetic approach to suppress MT activity during a motion discrimination task with post-decision wagering (PDW; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach.

claim: Very low light power levels were used to target relatively small clusters of excitatory neurons with similar selectivity for direction of motion.
source: While some primate optogenetics studies set out to illuminate the largest possible volume of tissue (Acker et al., 2016; Gerits et al., 2012), we used very low light power levels to target relatively small clusters of excitatory neurons with similar selectivity for direction of motion.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach, contrasting with other studies.

claim: In MT, small clusters of neurons with similar selectivity constitute a critical functional unit for the conversion of a sensory representation into evidence for the decision.
source: The rationale for this approach is that, in MT, such clusters constitute a critical functional unit for the conversion of a sensory representation into evidence for the decision.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional organization of MT that motivated the experimental approach.

claim: Optogenetic suppression was capable of inducing a choice bias against the neurons' preferred direction.
source: We found that optogenetic suppression was capable of inducing a choice bias against the neurons' preferred direction, and a qualitatively similar change in the pattern of post-decision wagering, broadly consistent with a common mechanism underlying choice and confidence.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the main behavioral findings.

claim: Optogenetic suppression induced a qualitatively similar change in the pattern of post-decision wagering, broadly consistent with a common mechanism underlying choice and confidence.
source: We found that optogenetic suppression was capable of inducing a choice bias against the neurons' preferred direction, and a qualitatively similar change in the pattern of post-decision wagering, broadly consistent with a common mechanism underlying choice and confidence.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the relationship between choice and confidence effects.

claim: There is intriguing evidence for compensatory changes in the readout of MT activity, on both the sub-second and tens-of-minutes time scales.
source: We also found intriguing evidence for compensatory changes in the readout of MT activity, on both the sub-second and tens-of-minutes time scales.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the temporal dynamics of compensation.

claim: The results highlight the importance of spatial and temporal specificity in causal interventions.
source: The results highlight the importance of spatial and temporal specificity in causal interventions, and they suggest a possible explanation for weak behavioral effects of optogenetic manipulations in some previous nonhuman primate studies.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The results suggest a possible explanation for weak behavioral effects of optogenetic manipulations in some previous nonhuman primate studies.
source: The results highlight the importance of spatial and temporal specificity in causal interventions, and they suggest a possible explanation for weak behavioral effects of optogenetic manipulations in some previous nonhuman primate studies.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: A red-shifted opsin was chosen for its superior photocurrent at very low irradiance.
source: Note that unlike previous studies, a red-shifted opsin was chosen not for its suitability for large-volume tissue illumination (Acker et al., 2016) but for its superior photocurrent at very low irradiance (Chuong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for choosing Jaws, supported by citations.

claim: Optrode design, laser power, and site selection criteria were all intended to limit the light-induced suppression of activity to a relatively small cluster of MT neurons with consistent receptive field and tuning properties.
source: Optrode design, laser power, and site selection criteria were all intended to limit the light-induced suppression of activity to a relatively small cluster of MT neurons with consistent receptive field and tuning properties (i.e., preferred speed and direction of motion).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Physiologically effective irradiance levels extended at most 300–500 µm from the fiber tip.
source: These estimates suggest that physiologically effective irradiance levels extended at most 300–500 µm from the fiber tip, which we confirmed qualitatively in pilot experiments using a fiber affixed to a linear electrode array (V-Probe, Plexon, Inc., Dallas, TX).
evidence: This is a statement about the spatial extent of photosuppression based on simulations and pilot experiments.

claim: The laser power was titrated to achieve an amount of suppression just shy of maximum (saturating) levels.
source: After identifying a candidate site, we titrated the laser power to achieve an amount of suppression just shy of maximum (saturating) levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: A handful of neurons showed no effect or an increase in firing rate in response to photosuppression.
source: Single-unit visual responses to high-coherence RDM stimuli—presented at the preferred direction and speed—were strongly suppressed on average (N = 26; Figure 3A), although a handful of neurons showed no effect or an increase in firing rate.
evidence: This is a direct observation about the variability in neural responses to photosuppression.

claim: The handful of cells showing no effect or increased firing rate presumably includes those that did not express Jaws, as well as a small minority that were indirectly activated through polysynaptic mechanisms.
source: Presumably this handful of cells includes those that did not express Jaws, as well as a small minority that were indirectly activated through polysynaptic mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference about the identity of neurons that did not show suppression.

claim: The fractional degree of suppression, calculated from MU activity, varied substantially both within and across sessions.
source: The fractional degree of suppression (Equation 4; Materials and methods), calculated from MU activity, varied substantially both within and across sessions (Figure 3A, inset; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation about the variability in neural suppression.

claim: A post-suppression rebound of activity was observed after turning off the laser (and visual stimulus).
source: A post-suppression rebound of activity was observed after turning off the laser (and visual stimulus).
evidence: This is a direct observation about neural activity following photosuppression.

claim: The rebound of spiking after abrupt laser offset is a known byproduct of photosuppression.
source: Note that the rebound of spiking after abrupt laser offset (Figure 3B), a known byproduct of photosuppression, was mitigated by introducing a 140 ms ramp-down of laser power in the majority of behavioral sessions (Figure 3D; Chuong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about a known phenomenon, supported by citation.

claim: No difference in behavioral effects was detected when the rebound was suppressed, compared to an earlier subset of sessions without the ramp-down.
source: We did not detect a difference in behavioral effects when the rebound was suppressed, compared to an earlier subset of sessions without the ramp-down (Figure 3D, inset), and therefore pooled all sessions for subsequent analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparison of behavioral effects with and without the ramp-down.

claim: Microstimulation in areas MT and MST altered choice and confidence in a manner that largely mimics a change in the motion strength.
source: Microstimulation in areas MT and MST altered choice and confidence in a manner that largely mimics a change in the motion strength, with a directionality predicted by the preferred direction of the stimulated neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings by the authors.

claim: The direction and size of shifts in choice and confidence induced by µStim were well matched in the aggregate, and highly correlated across sessions.
source: The direction and size of these shifts in the previous study were well matched in the aggregate, and highly correlated across sessions, suggesting that MT/MST activity contributes to a common decision variable that governs both choice and confidence (Fetsch et al., 2014a; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: MT/MST activity contributes to a common decision variable that governs both choice and confidence.
source: The direction and size of these shifts in the previous study were well matched in the aggregate, and highly correlated across sessions, suggesting that MT/MST activity contributes to a common decision variable that governs both choice and confidence (Fetsch et al., 2014a; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009).

claim: Under the interpretation that MT/MST activity contributes to a common decision variable, suppression of MT activity should cause shifts in the opposite direction to µStim: fewer choices in the preferred direction, and a rightward shift of the bell-shaped confidence function.
source: Under this interpretation, suppression of MT activity—provided it is targeted to a population of neurons that share a common tuning preference—should cause shifts in the opposite direction: fewer choices in the preferred direction, and a rightward shift of the bell-shaped confidence function.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the theoretical framework and previous findings.

claim: Behavioral effects of photosuppression depend on the degree of suppression.
source: Moreover, one would expect behavioral effects to depend on the degree of suppression, which as noted above, was highly variable.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the theoretical framework and observed variability in suppression.

claim: The behavioral shifts on a selected group of control trials with matching ∆R (less than -0.45) were significantly smaller than the effects shown for actual photosuppression (p<10−5 for choice and p = 0.02 for confidence).
source: In direct comparison with the effects shown in Figure 4C–D, the behavioral shifts on a selected group of control trials with matching ∆R (i.e., less than -0.45) were significantly smaller (p<10−5 for choice and p = 0.02 for confidence).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the comparison between actual photosuppression and control trials.

claim: The behavioral effects observed under strong photosuppression cannot be explained away by normal response variability and its covariation with choice (and confidence).
source: This result implies that the behavioral effects we observed under strong photosuppression cannot be explained away by normal response variability and its covariation with choice (and confidence).

claim: Most individual sessions failed to show statistically reliable effects on behavior when analyzed in their entirety.
source: Indeed, most individual sessions failed to show statistically reliable effects on behavior when analyzed in their entirety (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).

claim: Salzman et al. (1992) reported that the effects of µStim dissipated over the course of the behavioral sessions, which they interpreted as indicating neuronal fatigue, damage, or shifts in the position of the stimulating electrode.

claim: At the conclusion of a subset of sessions, little evidence was found for optrode drift, tissue damage or response fatigue.
source: At the conclusion of a subset of sessions, we re-measured direction tuning at multiple depths and found little evidence for optrode drift, tissue damage or response fatigue.
evidence: This is a direct statement about control measurements performed at the end of sessions.

claim: The effect on confidence appears to dissipate more quickly than the effect on choice.
source: Interestingly, the effect on confidence (blue trace) appears to dissipate more quickly than the effect on choice, and 'overshoots' zero for a period of time roughly between trial numbers 500–800 (~40–65 min), before settling back to zero later in the session (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct observation about the temporal dynamics of behavioral effects.

claim: Positive values on the ordinate (indicating leftward shifts of the function) are opposite of the expected effect from inactivation and were observed previously with µStim.
source: Note that positive values on the ordinate indicate leftward shifts of the function, as observed previously with µStim, and are thus opposite of the expected effect from inactivation.
evidence: This is a clarification about the interpretation of the data in relation to previous findings.

claim: The trend toward a transient overshoot in the confidence effect was not statistically significant (p=0.14).
source: Although the trend was not statistically significant (p=0.14; Equation 3 applied to trial numbers 550–750), it raises the possibility of a dissociation between choice and confidence on this particular subset of trials (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the statistical significance of an observed trend.

claim: The trend toward a transient overshoot raises the possibility of a dissociation between choice and confidence on this particular subset of trials.

claim: Weaker direction selectivity was observed during the latter half of the stimulus presentation on long-duration trials.
source: We did observe weaker direction selectivity during the latter half of the stimulus presentation on long-duration trials (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is a direct observation about neural responses on long-duration trials.

claim: It is conceivable that late epochs of neural activity contributed less to behavior, under the assumption that neural signals contribute in proportion to their sensitivity or informativeness.

claim: It seems improbable that downstream circuits could treat early activity differently on short versus long trials, because at any given time during a trial there would be no way to predict whether the stimulus (and laser) would terminate in the next moment or continue.

claim: Nonhuman primate neuroscience has lacked an inactivation counterpart to electrical microstimulation with comparable spatial and temporal specificity.
source: This is the scale at which electrical microstimulation has proven most effective, but nonhuman primate neuroscience has lacked an inactivation counterpart with comparable spatial and temporal specificity, relying on pharmacological and cooling methods that persist for minutes to days and affect larger swaths of tissue (but see Afraz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citation.

claim: There is justifiable excitement surrounding the development of optogenetic methods for targeting particular cell types or anatomical projections.
source: There is justifiable excitement surrounding the development of optogenetic methods for targeting particular cell types or anatomical projections (El-Shamayleh et al., 2017; Klein et al., 2016; Stauffer et al., 2016; Ohayon, 2017), and many questions will require such an approach.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citations.

claim: Another form of targeting—that of spatially or topographically organized populations—is viable in monkeys using off-the-shelf viral vectors combined with careful site selection and light delivery.

claim: Decision confidence is defined as the subjective degree of belief that one has chosen the correct or more rewarding option among alternatives.

source: In many natural situations, the decision maker does not receive immediate feedback on the accuracy of a choice, but instead must rely on confidence to guide subsequent decisions that depend on previous outcomes (Averbeck, 2015; van den Berg et al., 2016b).

claim: Confidence has a powerful influence on learning and adapting to new environments.
source: Confidence also has a powerful influence on learning and adapting to new environments.

claim: When negative feedback follows a choice made with high confidence, it implies that something about the world has changed, triggering a shift in behavioral strategy or an increase in learning rate.
source: For instance, when negative feedback follows a choice made with high confidence, it implies that something about the world has changed, triggering a shift in behavioral strategy or an increase in learning rate (Purcell and Kiani, 2016; Yu and Dayan, 2005).

claim: One class of hypotheses asserts that the processing of the evidence that supports a choice simultaneously furnishes an assessment of the reliability of the source of evidence, and hence a prediction about whether the choice will be correct.
source: One class of hypotheses asserts that the processing of the evidence that supports a choice simultaneously furnishes an assessment of the reliability of the source of evidence, and hence a prediction about whether the choice will be correct (for reviews see Fetsch et al., 2014b; Kepecs and Mainen, 2012; Meyniel et al., 2015; Pouget et al., 2016; Yeung and Summerfield, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about theoretical models of confidence, supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Kiani and Shadlen (2009) demonstrated how choice, reaction time, and confidence can arise through a common mechanism of evidence accumulation.
source: In this vein, Kiani and Shadlen (2009) demonstrated how choice, reaction time, and confidence can arise through a common mechanism of evidence accumulation, and several studies have since provided additional support for this idea (Fetsch et al., 2014a; Kiani et al., 2014; van den Berg et al., 2016a; Zylberberg et al., 2016).

claim: Changes in both choice and confidence measures under MT/MST microstimulation evinced a commensurate change in the strength of momentary evidence.
source: Changes in both measures—and their specific relationship with motion strength and viewing duration—evinced a commensurate change in the strength of momentary evidence, and the improvement in discrimination sensitivity when confidence was high (i.e., Figure 1C) was retained, as predicted by a bounded evidence accumulation model.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings by the authors.

claim: The improvement in discrimination sensitivity when confidence was high was retained under MT/MST microstimulation, as predicted by a bounded evidence accumulation model.
source: Changes in both measures—and their specific relationship with motion strength and viewing duration—evinced a commensurate change in the strength of momentary evidence, and the improvement in discrimination sensitivity when confidence was high (i.e., Figure 1C) was retained, as predicted by a bounded evidence accumulation model.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings by the authors and their consistency with theoretical predictions.

claim: Photosuppression may have caused both a bias and an increase in discrimination sensitivity by improving the signal-to-noise, just as µStim appeared to reduce it.
source: Interestingly, these observations can be reconciled in a bounded accumulation framework, the interpretation being that photosuppression caused both a bias and an increase in discrimination sensitivity by improving the signal-to-noise, just as µStim appeared to reduce it (Fetsch et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data based on a theoretical framework and comparison to previous findings.

claim: The data set lacks sufficient power to conclusively support or reject the possibility that photosuppression caused both a bias and an increase in discrimination sensitivity.
source: Our data set lacks sufficient power to conclusively support or reject this possibility, but if borne out by additional experiments, it would be within a family of previously observed alterations to signal and noise that jointly affect confidence and choice in a manner predicted by bounded accumulation (Zylberberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current data set.

claim: If photosuppression caused both a bias and an increase in discrimination sensitivity, it would be within a family of previously observed alterations to signal and noise that jointly affect confidence and choice in a manner predicted by bounded accumulation.
source: Our data set lacks sufficient power to conclusively support or reject this possibility, but if borne out by additional experiments, it would be within a family of previously observed alterations to signal and noise that jointly affect confidence and choice in a manner predicted by bounded accumulation (Zylberberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about how the findings would fit into the broader literature, supported by citation.

claim: The size of the effect on choices tended to be greater on trials without the sure-bet option available, compared to when it was available.
source: Lastly, the size of the effect on choices tended to be greater on trials without the sure-bet option available, compared to when it was available (data not shown), which was not the case for µStim (Fetsch et al., 2014b).

claim: None of the subtle discrepancies between choice and confidence effects reached statistical significance.
source: None of these discrepancies reached statistical significance, but taken together, they suggest the possibility that the neural substrates of choice and confidence might be partly dissociable at the level of the representation of sensory evidence.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical significance of observed trends.

claim: Taken together, subtle discrepancies between choice and confidence effects suggest the possibility that the neural substrates of choice and confidence might be partly dissociable at the level of the representation of sensory evidence.

claim: In general, a pure choice bias will tend to increase the error rate.
source: In general, a pure choice bias will tend to increase the error rate, so a mechanism that detects and counteracts the bias could be beneficial in terms of maximizing reward.

claim: The compensation must be induced by the suppression itself and initiated within a few tenths of a second, since different durations were randomly interleaved.
source: This observation is surprising because the different durations were randomly interleaved, suggesting that the compensation must be induced by the suppression itself and initiated within a few tenths of a second.

claim: The fast compensation is not a trivial consequence of the brain placing greater weight on sensory evidence arriving earlier within a trial.
source: We do not know how this fast compensation comes about, but it is not a trivial consequence of the brain placing greater weight on sensory evidence arriving earlier within a trial (e.g., Kiani et al., 2008; Raposo et al., 2012), since early MT activity is suppressed to the same degree on long versus short trials (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is a statement ruling out a particular explanation, supported by data and citations.

claim: The suppression of cortical tissue might have an effect analogous to diaschisis, triggering a reconfiguration of functional connectivity in downstream networks.
source: That is, unlike µStim, the suppression of cortical tissue might have an effect that is analogous to diaschisis (Carrera and Tononi, 2014; Otchy et al., 2015), triggering a reconfiguration of functional connectivity in downstream networks.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on comparison to diaschisis and cited literature.

claim: Initially compensation happens only after the first few hundred ms within a trial, then gradually the readout becomes able to rely on alternative signals from the start of the trial.
source: Initially this happens only after the first few hundred ms within a trial, then gradually the readout becomes able to rely on these signals from the start of the trial, resulting in late trials showing no effect of suppression even when limiting the analysis to short durations (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the temporal dynamics of compensation.

claim: The account of fast compensation is admittedly speculative.
source: This account is admittedly speculative, but it may suggest an opportunity for filling a major gap in our understanding, namely how information is dynamically routed from a multitude of possible sources (both sensory and mnemonic; Shadlen and Shohamy, 2016) to the circuits responsible for decision and action.
